title: Jeremiah 13:12–14
context: Jeremiah 13:12–14 is a short saying the LORD gives Jeremiah to speak. He is to say, “Every container should be filled with wine”, a proverb-like line the people answer as obvious (13:12). The LORD then explains that he will fill all the inhabitants of the land, including the kings who sit on David’s throne, the priests, the prophets, and the people of Jerusalem, with drunkenness, and dash them one against another without pity (13:13–14). Readers commonly take the drunkenness as an image of helpless confusion under judgment, and the passage may be read alongside the cup of wrath in 25:15, “Take this cup of the wine of wrath from my hand”, named here without harmonizing. The severity of 13:14 belongs to a prophetic announcement of judgment and is read in both traditions alongside the calls to repentance that follow in 13:15–17. Questions about how God uses hostile powers in judgment are treated in the existing box at Judges 9:23.

verses.text: “Therefore you shall speak to them this word: ‘The LORD, the God of Israel says, “Every container should be filled with wine.” ’ They will tell you, ‘Do we not certainly know that every container should be filled with wine?’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah to say, “Every container should be filled with wine”, and the people answer that they certainly know this. Arminian readers note that the saying sounds like a common proverb, perhaps a cheerful one, and they see the LORD turning it into a warning the people do not expect.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same use of a familiar saying and read the people’s dismissive reply as part of their failure to listen. They observe that prophets often take ordinary words and give them an unexpected meaning in order to awaken a complacent audience.

verses.text: Then tell them, ‘The LORD says, “Behold, I will fill all the inhabitants of this land, even the kings who sit on David’s throne, the priests, the prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, with drunkenness.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will fill all the inhabitants of the land, including the kings, priests, prophets, and people of Jerusalem, with drunkenness. Arminian readers note that the drunkenness pictures confusion and helplessness under judgment, and that every level of society is included.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same image and compare the cup of wrath in 25:15, named here without harmonizing. They observe that the judgment reaches the kings who sit on David’s throne, which shows that the Davidic line was not exempt from covenant discipline, while God’s promises to David remain.

verses.text: I will dash them one against another, even the fathers and the sons together,” says the LORD: “I will not pity, spare, or have compassion, that I should not destroy them.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I will dash them one against another, even the fathers and the sons together”, and that he will not pity or spare. Arminian readers note the severity of the language and read it as a prophetic announcement of judgment that still stands alongside the call to hear in 13:15–17.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same severity and read it as the just sentence on persistent rebellion. They observe that the announcement is set beside appeals to repent in the following verses, and both traditions read it in that setting rather than as the whole of God’s word to his people.
